On this page

How it works ​

The assistant is one long-running agent with a single session per account, working one turn at a time. This page is the mechanism overview; the full detail is the repository's docs/how-it-works.md and this page links to it rather than repeating it.

What starts a turn ​

  • Messages. A private message, or a group message that @s the assistant, replies to it or names it, starts a turn according to that conversation's policy; other group messages may start one when it decides to join in.
  • Wake words. When it ends a turn quietly, it can arm a few words; for six hours, any of them in that conversation starts a new turn.
  • wait. It can say "look again in a while", from one minute to one day; when the time comes the conversation reopens with its newest messages.
  • Scheduled tasks. Set in an admin's private chat, each opening a turn in a chosen conversation with the task's note as its input.
  • Free turns. When a set number of minutes passes with no turn at all, it gets a turn of its own that belongs to no conversation. Off by default; the interval is set on Advanced.

One batch, one decision ​

Messages are collected briefly first: longer while the same person keeps typing, shorter when someone else answers, at most a second when it is @'d, never more than about eight seconds for a whole batch. In a group, Jev scores whether joining in is natural; the stack subtracts a small penalty when it has just been talking, a little less when the batch @s it. After a few batches in a row where it stayed out, the next check waits longer - messages are held, not dropped. When several conversations are waiting, the one that has waited too long goes first, and Jev may reorder the rest by urgency.

One session, rotating windows ​

The working memory is not one transcript that grows forever. It is a sequence of context windows, each with a token budget, and a window is replaced when tokens - never a turn count - say so. While a window is open its beginning never changes, which keeps the model provider's prompt cache valid. As a window fills, the stack sends staged reminders that ask it to write notes and prepare a handoff; at the hard limit the stack rolls over by itself. A new window opens with a fixed opening note, the active notes, the handoff and the chat's recent messages; the previous window is not replayed, but its notes, its own history and the chat log all stay reachable.

Notes: the only long-term memory ​

Notes are written by the assistant itself; each carries a summary of at most 200 characters and a share of the token budget. Every new window keeps an active set

  • the pinned notes, the notes written or edited in the closing window, then the rest by measured usage - and everything else stays archived and searchable. Notes are append-only and anchored to the messages and actions they came from, so a note keeps pointing at its sources after it is edited. Browse them on Memory.

Jev: yes/no judgments ​

Jev is TypeSafe AI's decision model.

Jev never writes replies; it answers short yes/no questions with a probability, and the stack compares that against a threshold. It is used for joining in, reply timing, quoting, queue order, the review of every outbound bubble, the network gate for a domain on neither list, and which notes stay active at rollover. Each decision has its own mode - off, shadow (asked and logged, the plain rule still acts) or on - and a new decision ships in shadow.

Compared with other projects ​

The side-by-side comparison of the context handling (AstrBot, MaiBot, DeepSeek Harness and pi) is the last part of docs/how-it-works.md.
